bull_bear.body:
- Quality and MRL-compliance leadership: 'Our commitment to producing high quality, MRL compliant teas has consistently positioned us at the top of the industry', with both domestic and international buyers recognising the Company as a sustainable and reliable business partner
- Realisation premium: average realisations in both the Orthodox and CTC categories remained significantly higher than the Assam Valley industry averages despite a softer pricing environment
- Manufacturing flexibility to switch between Orthodox and CTC production, allowing quick adaptation to market dynamics
- Long-standing customer and importer relationships in the UK, Germany and the Middle East, who recognise Rossell as a reliable and established supplier adhering to quality and MRL standards
- Enlarged production base after the acquisition of Dhoedaam, taking the Company to seven tea estates and delivering its highest-ever total tea production and turnover
- Rossell Tea is regarded as a benchmark for quality in both the Orthodox and CTC categories among domestic and international customers
- Sustainability credentials - Rainforest Alliance certified CTC estates, solar power infrastructure across four estates, regenerative agricultural practices, and an in-house bio-formulation production unit
- Established workforce and estate community practices - a workforce of over 13,000 employees, cordial industrial relations across all units, and recognition by Government and other authorities for statutory compliance and employee welfare
bull_bear.title: Bull — competitive strengths

bull_bear.body:
- Climate and weather dependence of an agricultural crop — Tea is an agricultural product wholly dependent on weather; global climatic change has made conditions erratic and unpredictable, and extreme weather impacts both crop and quality. El Nino-induced weather extremes continue to hit crop yields despite afforestation, irrigation and flood-control mitigation, and BRSR identifies Climate Change as a material risk with negative financial implications. During the year, low rainfall and inclement weather cut production at the Nagrijuli, Kharikatia and Dhoedaam estates, and inadequate, delayed rainfall in Upper Assam and the North Bank produced poor cropping from January to March 2026.
- Pest and disease pressure with shrinking chemical options — Climate change is bringing new pests and diseases, incidence has increased and some pests have become resistant to existing pesticides. With chemical options constrained by residue limits, the Company relies on bio formulations, whose effectiveness falls in extreme weather and whose availability in the required quantity and quality in the local market remains a challenge - the reason it has started its own production unit at Romai Tea Estate.
- Regulatory / MRL compliance risk in export markets — Strict international MRL standards and certifications add complexity to exports. The EU's stricter Maximum Residue Limits for neonicotinoids, and inconsistent chemical usage among small growers, threaten export viability and domestic production; the evolving EU-2026 MRL requirements are expected to increase compliance challenges globally, and remaining compliant with the new 2026 MRL regime is named as a specific challenge for UK/Europe exports. Strict EU MRL rules are cited as threatening some 40M kg of Indian exports, with costly compliance testing.
- Geopolitical and macroeconomic disruption to trade and input costs — Ongoing wars (Russia-Ukraine, West Asia), India-Pakistan tensions and global inflation have led to weaker demand, volatile pricing and increased shipping costs. Input costs for fuel, gas, fertilizers, packaging materials and food have risen sharply following the conflicts in West Asia and the near three-month closure of the Strait of Hormuz, while Red Sea shipping is yet to normalise and freight and insurance costs have risen significantly.
- Import competition and export price competitiveness — Rising imports of lower-cost teas from Kenya, Nepal and other producing countries pressure domestic pricing and export competitiveness; lower prevailing Kenyan prices are encouraging overseas buyers to shift part of their sourcing to that market, and a price imbalance between Indian and African CTC teas, alongside sluggish global trade, continues to affect competitiveness.
- Tea price cyclicality and demand softness, particularly in CTC — Domestic tea prices are largely driven by supply-demand dynamics and periods of over-production can result in lower market realisations. CTC demand remained subdued on weaker demand from domestic buyers including large packeteers; the CTC market was subdued from April to November 2025 with prices declining significantly in August and September 2025, and prices in both CTC and Orthodox categories were lower than the previous year.
- Cost inflation, especially wages and fuel — Management identifies reining in escalating costs, particularly wages and fuel, as the biggest challenge alongside protecting the crop; a staff salary increase took effect from 1st April 2025 and was absorbed only through higher production and product mix.
- Occupational health and safety on estates — BRSR identifies Occupational Health & Safety as a material risk with negative financial implications: tea cultivation and processing expose workers to manual labour, machinery and agrochemical use, mitigated through regular safety audits and drills, awareness sessions on safe handling of equipment and chemicals, PPE distribution and strict adherence to OHS protocols.
- Substitution and changing consumer preference in end markets — Competition from coffee, energy drinks and other beverage categories in key international markets, inflationary pressure on consumer spending and value-volume growth, and sustainability demands pushing brands toward organic and eco-friendly packaging are flagged as consumption-side risks.
bull_bear.title: Bear — key risks

business.body: Rossell India Limited, operating as Rossell Tea, is engaged in the cultivation, manufacture and sale of tea, with its gross revenue from operations arising from the sale of tea and black pepper. It manufactures both Orthodox and CTC black tea from its own leaf across seven tea estates in Assam, supplemented by bought (outsourced) leaf, and retains the flexibility to switch between Orthodox and CTC manufacture as markets move. The Rossell Tea Division supplies tea primarily to institutional buyers and trade partners such as auction buyers, tea blending and packaging companies, branded tea manufacturers and exporters, who use Rossell's teas for blending, packaging and distribution in domestic and international markets; exports constitute 25.09% of the total turnover of the entity.

outlook.body:
- Compete on quality and compliance rather than volume - 'Quality and compliance will continue to be our guiding principles', with a commitment to producing the highest-quality CTC and Orthodox teas and maintaining the compliance standards that differentiate Rossell Tea in domestic and international markets
- Leverage MRL compliance as a competitive advantage: with MRL compliance becoming increasingly critical, the Company sees an opportunity to further strengthen long-term associations with buyers
- Grow export volumes by leveraging favourable exchange rates and expanding global reach; the weak rupee is expected to offset some export challenges by enhancing earnings from foreign markets
- Widen the export customer base - continuing engagement with existing customers in the UK, Germany and the Middle East while establishing new contacts with buyers in the USA and Canada
- Use manufacturing flexibility between Orthodox and CTC to adapt quickly to market dynamics, and convert all bought leaf into Orthodox tea to achieve higher average realisations
- Deepen sustainability credentials - extending Rainforest Alliance certification to Dhoedaam to take RA-certified CTC estates to four
- Practise sustainable agriculture (irrigation, drainage, shade planting, water bodies and rainwater harvesting) to mitigate erratic weather, and expand in-house bio-formulation production from Romai Tea Estate to other estates to manage pest and disease pressure without chemical options
- Work closely with industry associations and regulatory bodies on sustainable practices and quality enhancement to address geopolitical, climatic, regulatory and trade risks
- The Company distributes profit under a Dividend Distribution Policy approved by the Board of Directors on 9th February, 2022 and published on its website, with the Board recommending dividend each year in accordance with that policy; for the year under review the recommended payout was held at the same percentage of paid-up equity share capital as the previous year, and is placed before Members for declaration at the Annual General Meeting. Profit after tax is split between an appropriation to General Reserve under the first proviso to Section 123(1) of the Companies Act, 2013 and earnings retained in the business, reflecting a part-distribution, part-reinvestment stance. The equity base was unchanged during the year - no shares with differential voting rights, employee stock options or sweat equity shares were issued, and the Company has no convertible instruments. Structurally, the Company is a single standalone entity: it has no holding, subsidiary, associate company or joint venture as on the date of the Report, so all capital is deployed within the listed entity itself. Members are also being asked to approve, by Special Resolution, that managerial remuneration may exceed the overall limits stipulated under Section 197 of the Companies Act, 2013.
- Water management identified as a material opportunity: rainwater harvesting systems and check points within the estates, plus regular monitoring of water usage and conservation awareness among estate staff
- Climate-change mitigation through regenerative agriculture: Regen Agri projects for rejuvenation of soils, and production and application of Biochar for soil improvement
- Structured drainage systems during heavy rainfall to prevent waterlogging and minimise root rot and pest infestation, and timely irrigation when temperatures rise
- Climate resilience through maintaining water bodies and planting shade and fuel trees across the estates to improve the local microclimate and soil structure
- Creation of water bodies to mitigate drought and rainwater harvesting during the rains as part of sustainable agriculture practices (irrigation, drainage, shade planting)
- Pest outbreaks managed using only approved pesticides in strict compliance with agro-environmental norms, with increased use of bio formulations supported by the Company's own bio-formulation production unit at Romai Tea Estate, to be expanded to other estates
- Rainforest Alliance certification of CTC estates, with Dhoedaam soon to be certified taking the RA-certified count to four, reinforcing sustainability credentials
- Occupational health and safety programme: regular safety audits and drills, awareness sessions on safe handling of equipment and chemicals, PPE distribution to workers and strict adherence to OHS protocols
- Training and skill development identified as a material opportunity: induction programmes for new team members covering company ethos, workplace safety and ethical standards, and upskilling sessions for field operations, manufacturing efficiency and sustainable agricultural practices
- Grievance redressal mechanisms in place for communities, investors, shareholders, employees and workers, customers and value chain partners, with Estate Managers acting as primary liaisons for local communities and the Stakeholders' Relationship Committee overseeing investor and shareholder matters; policies and mechanisms published on the Company's website
- CSR is applicable to the Company under Section 135 of the Companies Act, 2013
outlook.title: Strategy & capital allocation

outlook.body: Rossell India's expansion during the year was acquisition-led rather than greenfield. The acquisition of Dhoedaam Tea Estate in January 2025 strengthened the Company's production base and took it to seven tea estates; Dhoedaam contributed 16.52 lakh kgs of made tea and was the principal reason CTC production and total turnover reached their highest-ever levels, while own-crop production across the six existing estates was broadly maintained. To build on that footprint, the Company has set up an Orthodox manufacturing facility at the Dhoedaam estate to increase production and boost revenue, positioning it to capture the buoyant Orthodox market, and expects to capitalise on the CTC market through improved quality delivery from Dhoedaam. Dhoedaam is also soon to be Rainforest Alliance certified, which will take the number of RA-certified CTC estates to four and enhance the Company's offer base. On the agronomy side, the Company has commissioned its own bio-formulation production unit at Romai Tea Estate to ensure timely supply of adequate quantity and quality of bio formulations, and states it will expand this to other estates as well. Supporting climate-resilience investments include creation of water bodies and rainwater harvesting infrastructure across the estates. No capex outlay, capacity figure or commissioning schedule is disclosed in the sections provided.
outlook.title: Capex & expansion plans

outlook.body:
- Lower Indian and Sri Lankan Orthodox crop plus the price differential between Indian and Sri Lankan Orthodox is working in the Company's favour, driving strong demand particularly from buyers in the Middle East and CIS regions
- Management expects the Indian Orthodox market, buoyant since the start of the year, to remain firm through the year with good demand from the CIS and Middle East; lower production in India and Sri Lanka is expected to give a fillip to prices
- Looking ahead, management sees production in India being marginally higher though global tea production may be slightly lower; CTC prices may be somewhat similar to last year but marginally better for the Company owing to its compliance and quality, while Orthodox prices will be better than the previous year
- Sri Lankan auction prices remain about Rs. 10-20 above prevailing Indian Orthodox prices, which management says provides an opportunity for Rossell to fill the gap
- Good quality and compliant CTC is expected to continue to sell at remunerative prices, while anything below good will decline in price as arrivals increase - a mix/quality-led realisation lever
- CTC demand remains subdued because of weaker demand from domestic buyers including large packeteers, with dust prices well below brokens as large packeteers are not yet active; inflationary pressures appear to be affecting demand
- Global tea consumption is steadily rising but the consumption pattern is shifting towards health-conscious, functional and ready-to-drink formats, with green tea gaining share globally
- Product mix, efficiencies and productivity, together with higher production lowering unit cost, helped absorb the staff salary increase effective 1st April 2025
- The biggest challenge ahead is to protect the crop and rein in escalating costs, particularly wages and fuel; a further challenge for UK/Europe exports is remaining compliant with the new MRL regime of 2026
- Increased imports of lower-cost teas from Kenya and other producing countries continue to pressure domestic pricing and export competitiveness, with lower Kenyan prices encouraging overseas buyers to shift part of their sourcing
- Management states it is 'very hopeful that with progress of the season, we would be able to procure more export orders from Germany, UAE, UK, and Saudi Arabia and also maybe from USA and Canada' - a qualitative export order pipeline, with no order-book value disclosed

The Company has established new contacts with buyers in the USA and Canada and expects to procure more export orders from Germany, UAE, UK and Saudi Arabia as the season progresses.
Management flags that the biggest challenge ahead will be to protect the crop and rein in escalating costs, particularly wages and fuel.
A further challenge for exports to the UK/Europe will be to remain compliant with the new MRL regime of 2026, which is expected to increase compliance challenges for tea producers globally.
The Company intends to capitalise on remunerative prices for good quality and compliant CTC through improved quality delivery from Dhoedaam.
Dhoedaam Tea Estate is soon to be Rainforest Alliance certified, which will take the Company's RA-certified CTC estates to four and enhance its offer base.
The Company aims to achieve higher export volumes by leveraging favourable exchange rates and expanding its global reach.
